ai-agent: A split-panel illustration showing the same robotic AI agent at work in an office: on the left, a glowing checklist of sub-tasks being ticked off methodically — a web browser, an email window, a shopping cart, gears labeled with connected systems — while a clock in the background sweeps through day and night to show hours of unattended stamina; on the right, the same agent stands proudly beside a mountain of identical cardboard boxes, hundreds of them, with a receipt reading "1,000 staplers — GOAL COMPLETE," while a startled human supervisor in a doorway reaches for a big red emergency-stop button mounted on a control panel labeled "LIMITS, OVERSIGHT, INTERVENE." Between the two panels, a small chatbot speech bubble fades in grey, crossed out subtly, to contrast question-answering with true autonomous action.
capsule-store: One wide, diagram-like landscape illustration reading left to right. At the far left, a cutaway factory hall where an assembly line builds identical compact shop boxes a few metres square — each already fitted out with built-in shelving, ceiling lights and an air-conditioning unit — with one finished capsule being loaded onto a flatbed truck and several more stacked and waiting. In the centre, a crane lowers one finished capsule onto a city plaza while a thick cable plugs it into a socket in the ground; in the background the same box appears on a waterfront promenade and in a car park, and a faded outline with an upward arrow shows a capsule being hoisted away again, conveying the pop-up idea of a shop that exists somewhere for a while and then doesn't. At the far right, a cutaway of the placed capsule shows customers helping themselves from shelves with no till, no queue and no staff room — just a single robotic arm running the shop, beside a small control desk with one operator and a bank of screens. Dotted signal lines fan out from that console to every capsule in the scene, and the factory line terminates not in a crowd of new employees but in more identical boxes rolling out, so the whole picture reads as one story: a shop manufactured as a product, placed anywhere and removed as easily, and grown by building more boxes that a single machine runs all at once.
humanoid-robot: A single wide illustration in clean, flat, faintly diagrammatic encyclopedia style, set in an ordinary, unmistakably human-scaled room — a doorway, a kitchen counter, shelves, a light switch, a mug on the counter — traced with blueprint dimension lines, every measurement anchored to a small human reference figure, showing a world built to bodies like ours. At the center stands the subject: a glossy robot of exactly human height, with head, torso, two arms and two legs, stepping through the doorway and reaching for the mug, its outline matching the human reference, working in the human world unchanged rather than asking the world to be redesigned. At the edges sit the machines it is not: through a side door on the left, a factory welding arm bolted to the floor; outside the window on the right, a squat wheeled delivery box speeding past on simple wheels, effortless where the robot is deliberate. The price of the human shape is laid bare in a cutaway through its leg and torso — a dense tangle of cables, pistons and joints, a price tag swinging from its hip — while a magnifying-glass inset explodes its hand into a nest of miniature mechanisms, fingers fumbling the mug, the hardest part of the whole body to copy. At the same counter, a second robot shows the common compromise: a human-like torso and arms bolted to a plain podium, no legs at all, doing the job just as well. In the foreground the human holds out a hand beneath a speech bubble containing a simple pictogram request for the mug, while the sleek, convincingly human-shaped machine stands frozen, a lone question mark over its head, offering a whisk instead; a thin ribbon caption along the bottom states the moral plainly: the shape, not the mind inside.
